title: Lessons
body:
The Pine River watershed's contamination history offers three lessons the Task Force believes reach far beyond this community.

## 1. Respect the precautionary principle

Caution should guide the introduction of new products or methods until their long-term health and environmental impacts are understood. Dr. Irving Selikoff and Tony Mazzocchi pioneered this approach to occupational health policy, building on Bernardino Ramazzini (1633–1714), the Italian physician who first identified occupational hazards and called for precaution. The Collegium Ramazzini, founded by Selikoff and Dr. Cesare Maltoni, continues to bring together experts on occupational disease.

The Wingspread Statement (January 1998) put it plainly: precautionary measures should be taken even before cause and effect are fully established, and the burden of proof should fall on those proposing an activity, not on the public. Dr. Chris De Rosa (former Director for Toxicology, CDC/ATSDR) and Dr. Brenda Eskenazi (lead author of "The Pine River Statement," *Environmental Health Perspectives*) are among the experts who have applied this thinking to Pine River.

## 2. Practice responsible economics

Michigan Chemical/Velsicol operated in St. Louis for only 42 years (1936–1978) — yet cleanup has already taken longer than that, with remediation continuing indefinitely. The company never paid wages and taxes anywhere close to the eventual Superfund cleanup cost, before even counting the human health and ecological toll.

Economists Herman Daly (steady-state economics), Eleanor Ostrom (Nobel laureate, 2009, for her work on sustainable commons management), and Kate Raworth ("donut economics") offer frameworks for valuing resources the old model ignored. The International Society for Ecological Economics has published analysis of Pine River's regional remediation, and the Task Force sees its experience as validating Ostrom's principles: short-term corporate profit-taking creates long-term economic devastation for the community left holding the cleanup.

## 3. Become — and remain — good ancestors

Claims that the companies involved didn't know their operations were harmful don't hold up. Complaints, scientific warnings, and press coverage all preceded the worst of the pollution:

- 1935 — Saginaw City Council resolution on Pine River contamination; University of Michigan study on ecosystem degradation
- 1941 — 121 St. Louis residents formally complain about river harm
- 1945–1949 — *The New Yorker*, *The New Republic*, and peer-reviewed journals warn of DDT's dangers
- 1955 — Michigan Stream Control Commission documents contamination
- 1962 — Velsicol's attorneys threaten libel suits against Houghton Mifflin and *The New Yorker* over Rachel Carson's *Silent Spring*

Joseph Sowmick of the Saginaw Chippewa Tribe has reminded the Task Force that indigenous wisdom asks decision-makers to weigh impacts across seven generations. The Pine River community also shows a pattern common to environmental injustice — lower per-capita income and property values than the surrounding region — and the Task Force has partnered with similarly affected communities in Memphis, Detroit, Flint, and elsewhere.

**Further reading:** Roman Krznaric, *The Good Ancestor* (2020) and *History for Tomorrow* (2024/2025); Robert Bullard, *Dumping in Dixie* (1990); Benjamin Kline, *First Along the River* (5th ed., 2022); Naomi Oreskes & Erik Conway, *Merchants of Doubt* (2010).
